For this exercise, we will use the following two data sets.

1. `countries.txt`: A data set that contains a list of countries used in the paper "Implications of armed conflict for maternal and child health: A regression analysis of data from 181 countries for 2000–2019" and their three-digit ISO (International Organization for Standardization) code. 

2. `regions.txt`: A data set that contains a list of all major countries in the world and their
    a. ISO code (`country_code`)
    b. region (`region`)
    c. sub-region (`sub_region`)
    d. numerical region code (`region_code`)
    e. numerical sub-region code (`sub_region_code`)

```{r}
##  **Third**, subset the `regions` data set to only include countries from the `countries` data set.
## checking join 
# anti_join(countries, regions, by = c("ISO" = "country_code"))
# anti_join(regions, countries, by = c( "country_code" = "ISO"))
regions <- inner_join(regions, countries, by = c("country_code" = "ISO"))
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Tabulate countries by region and sub-region


```{r}
#Next, we want to find out how many countries are in a region. Use the `group_by()` and `summarise()` functions in the `dplyr` package to count the number of countries in each region. Then use the `kable()` function in the `knitr` package to create a simple table with the column headers, "Region" and "Count". 
regions |> group_by(region) |> summarise( n= n()) |> knitr::kable(
  col.names = c("Region", "Count"), caption = "Number of countries in each region")

# regions |> group_by(region) |> tally() |> knitr::kable(
#   col.names = c("Region", "Count"), caption = "Number of countries in each region")
```




```{r}
#Create a similar table that shows the number of countries in each **sub-region**.
regions |> group_by(sub_region) |> summarise( n= n())  |> knitr::kable(
  col.names = c("Subregion", "Count"), caption = "Number of countries in each subregion")
```


{{< pagebreak >}}

## Data visualization using ggplot 

```{r}
#| label: fig-country
#| fig-cap: Number of countries per subregion
library(ggplot2)
library(paletteer)

# Here, we will use `geom_bar()` function within `ggplot()` to create a bar chart that displays the **number of countries** in each **sub-region**. 

# 1. Color code each sub-region by **region**.
# 2. Create bars that run horizontally where sub-region names appear along the y-axis. 
# 3. Order the bars such that the sub-region with the most number countries appear at the top and the sub-region with the least number of countries appear at the bottom. 

regions |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(sub_region)), fill = region))+
  geom_bar() +
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(y = "Subregion", x = "Number of Countries", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) + 
          scale_fill_paletteer_d("ggsci::default_jco")
```

```{r}
# read in all other datasets 

infmor0 <- read.csv("../data/raw/infant_mortality.csv", header = TRUE)
matmor0 <- read.csv("../data/raw/maternal_mortality.csv", header = TRUE)
neomor0 <- read.csv("../data/raw/neonatal_mortality.csv", header = TRUE)
un5mor0 <- read.csv("../data/raw/under5_mortality.csv", header = TRUE)


```

```{r}
### write a function that pivot each dataset to longer
wbfun <- function(dataname, varname){
  dataname |>
    dplyr::select(iso, indicator, X2000:X2019) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("X"),
                 names_to = "year",
                 names_prefix = "X",
                 values_to = varname) |>
    mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) |>
    arrange(iso, year) |> 
    select(-indicator)
}

matmor <- wbfun(dataname = matmor0, varname = "matmor")
infmor <- wbfun(dataname = infmor0, varname = "infmor")
neomor <- wbfun(dataname = neomor0, varname = "neomor")
un5mor <- wbfun(dataname = un5mor0, varname = "un5mor")

#put all data frames into list
wblist <- list(matmor, infmor, neomor, un5mor)

#merge all data frames in list
wblist |> reduce(full_join, by = c('iso', 'year')) -> wbdata ## apply full join to each item in list iteratively 


```

```{r}
#prepare disaster data 
disaster0 <- read.csv("../data/raw/disaster.csv", header = TRUE)

disaster0 <- disaster0 |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

disaster <- disaster0 |> 
  filter(disaster_type == "Earthquake" | disaster_type == "Drought") |> 
  filter(year >= 2000 & year <= 2019) |> 
  select(iso, year, disaster_type)

disaster$event <- 1

disaster <- left_join( wbdata |> select(iso, year), disaster, by = c("iso", "year"))

disaster <- disaster |> mutate(
  event = ifelse(is.na(disaster_type), 0, event),
  disaster_type = ifelse(is.na(disaster_type), "Earthquake", disaster_type))


## create dummy variable of drought and earthquake per country per year
disaster <- disaster |> 
  distinct(iso, year, disaster_type, .keep_all = T) |> 
  pivot_wider(
  id_cols = c("iso", "year"), 
  names_from = disaster_type, 
  values_from = event, 
  values_fill = 0
)


```

```{r}
#prepare disaster data 
conflict <- read.csv("../data/raw/conflict.csv", header = TRUE)

conflict <- conflict |> 
  group_by(iso, year) |> 
  summarise(death_sum = sum(best, na.rm = T)) |> 
  mutate(conflict = ifelse(death_sum >= 25, 1, 0),  #binary variable indicating
# the presence of conflict for each country–year observation (0 = no, <25 battle-related
# deaths; 1 = yes, �25 battle-related deaths)
  year = year + 1) ## lag 1 year, eg year 1999 predicts deaths in year 2000  

```

```{r}
# merge all data 
data <- list(wbdata, disaster, conflict)

#merge all data frames in list
data |> reduce(full_join, by = c('iso', 'year')) -> data

write.csv(data, "../data/processed/data.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "")

head(data)


```
